candidates.name: US HTS tariff code classification from product descriptions
candidates.task: Input: a free-text product description (material, construction, function, use). Output: the 6-digit HTS subheading and the full 10-digit US HTS code, as CBP would assign it in a binding ruling.
candidates.why_hard_for_llm: The 10-digit level has about 2,992 codes in the ATLAS ruling set, and the tariff rules hinge on fine material and use distinctions. The best reported frontier model (GPT-5-Thinking, 2025) gets 25.0% of 10-digit codes fully right on the ATLAS 200-item test set, and the 6-digit level sits near 55%.
candidates.business_value: Customs brokers, importers and e-commerce sellers pay for correct duty rates; a misclassification means duty underpayment penalties or overpayment. Brokers today search CBP's CROSS rulings by hand before filing.

datasets.name: ATLAS CROSS rulings dataset (flexifyai/cross_rulings_hts_dataset_for_tariffs)
datasets.size: 18,731 rulings, 2,992 unique 10-digit codes; splits 18,254 train / 200 validation / 200 test (per ATLAS Table 1)
datasets.labels: 10-digit HTS code per product description; 6-digit derived
datasets.license: not verified (HF page returned HTTP 401 to the fetch tool; the arXiv paper is CC BY 4.0, which does not cover the dataset)
datasets.notes: The 401 suggests a login or gate; check the page in a browser before planning on it.

datasets.name: CBP CROSS rulings database (rulings.cbp.gov)
datasets.size: unverified (third-party sources say about 220,000 rulings back to 1989; not read on CBP's own page)
datasets.labels: Ruling text with the HTS classification it assigns
datasets.license: not verified (public government database; terms not read)
datasets.notes: Free search without an account, per third-party guides. Good source for building your own rows.

frontier_evidence.source: ATLAS: Benchmarking and Adapting LLMs for Global Trade via Harmonized Tariff Code Classification (Yuvraj & Devarakonda)
frontier_evidence.models_tested: GPT-5-Thinking, Gemini-2.5-Pro-Thinking, DeepSeek-R1 (05/28), GPT-OSS-120B, LLaMA-3.3-70B base, Atlas (LLaMA-3.3-70B fine-tuned). No Claude or Gemini 3 model tested.
frontier_evidence.finding: 10-digit fully correct: GPT-5-Thinking 25.0% (N=50/200), Gemini-2.5-Pro-Thinking 13.5%, DeepSeek-R1 2.5%, GPT-OSS-120B 1.5%, LLaMA-3.3-70B base 2.1%. 6-digit: GPT-5-Thinking 55.5%, Gemini 31.0%. The abstract's '+15' and '+27.5' gaps do not match the tables (Gemini gap is 26.5 from the tables); the paper gives no digit level for them.

frontier_evidence.source: A Deterministic Agentic Workflow for HS Tariff Classification (arXiv 2605.14857)
frontier_evidence.models_tested: Qwen3.6-plus (frontier-side reference), Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 non-thinking; evaluated on HSCodeComp
frontier_evidence.finding: Four-digit top-1 75.0% / top-3 91.5% and six-digit top-1 64.2% / top-3 78.3% for Qwen3.6-plus. Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 gives 84.2% four-digit and 77.4% six-digit top-1, but these measure agreement with the frontier model, not ground truth.

frontier_evidence.models_tested: agents built on frontier models (names not read)
frontier_evidence.finding: From a search snippet only: 632 products with expert 10-digit labels; strongest agent 46.8% against 95.0% for human experts. The PDF was too large for the fetch tool, so these numbers are unverified.

counterevidence.note: A fixed pipeline that confines LLM calls to narrow stages, with an offline-engineered rule base, gets 64.2% six-digit top-1 with a frontier model. This suggests the gap can close without training, through structure and rules. It weakens the 'LLM cannot do it' premise and strengthens the case for a tool-backed SLM as one stage, not the whole system.
At 6 digits the fine-tuned 70B model leads GPT-5-Thinking by 2 points (57.5 vs 55.5). The fine-tuning gain is large only at 10 digits (40.0 vs 25.0).

small_model_evidence.finding: Fine-tuning a 70B model lifts 10-digit fully-correct from 2.1% (base) to 40.0% and 6-digit from 20.7% to 57.5% on the 200-item test set. This is not small-model evidence: no model at 8B or below was reported. Note that Table 3 gives 20.7% for LLaMA base but N=29/200 is 14.5%; the paper is internally inconsistent here.
A 27B open model inside a deterministic pipeline reaches 77.4% six-digit top-1 against the frontier model's output (agreement, not ground truth). Still above 8B and not fine-tuned.

candidates.why_ft_beats_rag: Retrieving the CROSS rulings helps, but the skill is choosing among near-identical 10-digit codes after applying the Explanatory Notes; the ATLAS result (fine-tuning lifts 10-digit from about 2% to 40%) is the closest evidence that training on the labelled mapping matters more than adding context. This is a claim from the 70B model, not yet shown for a 1B–4B model.
candidates.example_input: Men's knitted cotton T-shirt, 100% cotton single jersey, 150 g/m2, crew neck, short sleeves, not for infants.
candidates.example_output: {"hts_6": "<6-digit subheading>", "hts_10": "<10-digit code as printed on the matched CROSS ruling>"} (illustrative; take real labels from the dataset rows, not from this text)
candidates.behavior_spec: For each held-out product description, the model returns one 10-digit HTS code that exactly matches the ruling's code; pass means exact match, and the 6-digit prefix is reported separately. Target: beat the prompted base at 10 digits on the same held-out set and sit above the ATLAS 40% line with 1B–4B weights.
candidates.agentic_demo: 1) Parse the product description into attributes (material, construction, use). 2) Call the USITC HTS search for chapter/heading candidates (third-party docs describe a reststop search endpoint; the official docs were not read). 3) Call CBP CROSS search for prior rulings on near-identical products. 4) SLM picks the 10-digit code from the candidate set and writes a one-line rationale citing the ruling number. 5) Human broker approval gate before any filing.
candidates.eval: Exact-match accuracy at 6 and 10 digits on a held-out ruling set, plus hierarchical partial credit (same chapter, same heading). Compare base model, tuned model and GPT-5 / Gemini on identical items with the same prompt family (zero-shot, few-shot, CoT) to satisfy the prompt-ceiling gate.
candidates.risks: The ATLAS test set is 200 items; the paper's own numbers conflict in places. Licence and access for the HF dataset are unverified (HTTP 401). Ground truth is CBP's rulings, which can be revoked or superseded by later rulings. Tariff schedules change yearly, so a tuned model goes stale.
candidates.qlora_feasibility: Data is ready in principle (18,254 train rows) and a 4-day timebox fits a 1B–4B QLoRA run. Main effort is verifying the dataset's licence and access, and checking that the rulings are in the year the model will be evaluated against.

candidates.name: XBRL / US-GAAP tagging of numeric facts in SEC filings
candidates.task: Input: a sentence or table cell from a 10-K or 10-Q that contains a number. Output: the US-GAAP concept (for example us-gaap:Revenues) the number should be tagged with. A two-stage version: first find and type the number, then link it to a concept.
candidates.why_hard_for_llm: The taxonomy has about 17,000 concepts, and close pairs differ only in a qualifier. FinTagging reports that LLMs extract numbers well but struggle with fine-grained concept linking: FinCL accuracy is 0.10–0.19 for the frontier and open LLMs it tested. The fine-tuned encoder baseline does not clearly beat them on the macro score.
candidates.business_value: Public companies and their filing agents pay for correct XBRL tags, since mis-tags cause SEC review and restatement cost. A tagging assistant cuts the manual time an accountant spends per filing.

datasets.name: FiNER-139 (nlpaueb/finer-139)
datasets.labels: 139 XBRL entity types, token-level IOB2 (279 token labels); gold tags from auditors, with some discrepancies noted on the card
datasets.notes: Sentences drawn from about 10k SEC filings; regex extraction of notes. Covers only the 139 most frequent entity types, not the full taxonomy.

datasets.name: FinTagging benchmark (TheFinAI/fintagging)
datasets.size: FinCL has 52,572 query-answer pairs over 17,388 concepts (paper text, from search snippet; the full-page read gave 17,688 concepts, so the two disagree)
datasets.labels: FinNI numeric entities with types; FinCL gold US-GAAP concept
datasets.license: not verified (the arXiv page is CC BY 4.0; the dataset licence was not stated on the page read)
datasets.notes: HF collection https://huggingface.co/collections/TheFinAI/fintagging linked from the paper; not opened.

frontier_evidence.source: FinTagging: Benchmarking LLMs for Extracting and Structuring Financial Information (arXiv 2505.20650)
frontier_evidence.models_tested: GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E, Llama-3.3-70B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, Qwen3-32B, gemma-2-27b, Qwen3-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-0.6B, Fino1-8B (zero-shot); fine-tuned BERT-large, FinBERT, SECBERT as baselines
frontier_evidence.finding: FinCL accuracy: GPT-4o 0.1829, DeepSeek-V3 0.1889, Qwen3-32B 0.1277, Llama-3.3-70B 0.1318. FinNI F1: GPT-4o 0.5397, DeepSeek-V3 0.6932. End-to-end pipeline accuracy: GPT-4o 0.1052, DeepSeek-V3 0.1074, Qwen3-32B 0.1127. Fine-tuned SECBERT Micro-F1 0.1779 vs DeepSeek-V3 0.1162, but Macro-F1 0.0203 vs DeepSeek-V3 0.0659.
XBRL auditing (detecting inconsistent tags), not tagging. Search snippet only: DeepSeek-V3 Hit Rate 11.89%, Recall 8.83%, Macro-F1 9.35%. Not read on the page.

counterevidence.source: Review verdict 'mostly missing knowledge of the taxonomy'
counterevidence.note: Partly disputed. FinTagging attributes the FinCL failure to fine-grained disambiguation among close taxonomy entries, not to unknown concepts. Its search-snippet summary also says accuracy stays low even with perfect candidate retrieval, so a lookup tool alone does not fix it. No ablation in the read material separates 'missing knowledge' from 'disambiguation difficulty'. The evidence supports 'hard to disambiguate', and it does not show that a tuned SLM would beat frontier models.

A retrieve-then-rank tool over the US-GAAP taxonomy is a plausible counter to the brief's 'RAG would not fix it' test. FinTagging's end-to-end result with perfect retrieval still reads as low, which is the evidence for the brief's test. Not yet tested here.

small_model_evidence.source: FiNER-139 (Loukas et al., ACL 2022): SEC-BERT variants fine-tuned
small_model_evidence.finding: Test entity-level Micro-F1 / Macro-F1: BiLSTM (words) 77.3 / 73.8; BERT+CRF 78.0 / 75.2; SEC-BERT-shape 82.1 / 80.1; SEC-BERT-num 80.4 / 78.9. These are encoder models (about 110M parameters), with no frontier LLM comparison. Table 4 vs Table 5 disagree on SEC-BERT micro-F1 (75.7 vs 78.8).

small_model_evidence.source: FinTagging: fine-tuned SECBERT vs zero-shot LLMs
small_model_evidence.finding: Fine-tuned SECBERT beats DeepSeek-V3 on Micro-F1 (0.1779 vs 0.1162) and loses on Macro-F1 (0.0203 vs 0.0659). A small model wins only on the frequent-label score, so the result is mixed.

candidates.why_ft_beats_rag: The skill is a learned mapping: which of 17,000 concepts a number belongs to depends on context and taxonomy conventions, not on a missing fact that retrieval can fetch. FiNER-139 shows that fine-tuning on 900k labelled sentences gives strong token tagging; FinTagging shows zero-shot LLMs struggle with the concept-linking step. Whether a tuned model fixes it is untested.
candidates.example_input: "Total net revenues were $4.2 million for the year ended December 31, 2024, compared with $3.9 million in 2023."
candidates.example_output: {"value": 4200000, "unit": "USD", "concept": "us-gaap:Revenues", "period": "FY2024"} (illustrative; the concept choice is what the model must learn)
candidates.behavior_spec: For each numeric span in a filing excerpt, the model returns the US-GAAP concept that matches the auditor's gold tag exactly; pass means exact concept match on held-out spans. Target: beat zero-shot frontier FinCL accuracy (about 0.18–0.19 in FinTagging) on the same split.
candidates.agentic_demo: 1) Parse the filing into numeric spans with the SLM (FinNI-style). 2) Query a US-GAAP taxonomy index (the taxonomy file, read as a tool) for candidate concepts. 3) SLM ranks the candidates and returns one concept with its evidence span. 4) A validator checks the concept exists in the taxonomy and the unit and period match. 5) Output an iXBRL-ready tag list for an accountant to approve.
candidates.eval: Exact concept match (FinCL accuracy) and span-level F1 (FinNI) against gold tags on FinTagging or FiNER-139 held-out splits. Compare base, tuned and frontier models with the same candidate list, so the test isolates the linking step.
candidates.risks: FiNER-139 is token tagging over 139 labels, which fits an encoder better than a generative 1B–4B model, so the SLM framing needs a justification. Gold labels contain auditor discrepancies (stated on the card). Taxonomy versions change between years. FinTagging dataset licence not verified.
candidates.qlora_feasibility: Data is large and ready (FiNER-139 about 1.1M rows; FinTagging on HF). A 4-day timebox fits a QLoRA run on a subset of FinCL or FiNER. The main risk is the design choice: a generative SLM versus an encoder, which the course rules may not allow.

candidates.name: Patent CPC/IPC subclass classification from application text
candidates.task: Input: a patent application's title, abstract and first claim. Output: the primary CPC subclass (four-character code, for example H04L) for that application.
candidates.why_hard_for_llm: Zero-shot frontier models do poorly on exact CPC codes: IPBench reports CPC exact-match of 9.5% for DeepSeek-V3, 8.5% for DeepSeek-R1 and 3.3% for GPT-4o. The gap is in the fine-grained code, not the broad section. The labels are long-tail and hierarchical, and the examiner's choice is not always reproducible from text.
candidates.business_value: Patent firms and in-house IP teams pay for correct classification to route applications to examiners, run prior-art searches and set docketing. A tagging assistant cuts manual triage time.

datasets.name: HUPD (HUPD/hupd)
datasets.size: Card gives 125 GB total file size; no record count stated on the card. Filings from Jan 2004 to Dec 2018 (about 4.5M per the paper's text, not read on the card).
datasets.labels: main_cpc_label, cpc_labels, main_ipcr_label, ipcr_labels, decision (34 fields per application)
datasets.license: Conflict: YAML says cc-by-sa-4.0; the card body says 'released under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International'. Treat as unresolved.
datasets.notes: Dataset viewer disabled; loading needs Python code execution. The 'sample' config is small and 'all' is the full set.

datasets.name: USPTO-70k (named in search snippets for 2601.23200)
datasets.notes: The fetched 2601.23200 abstract page does not name the dataset, so the USPTO-70k link is unconfirmed.

frontier_evidence.source: IPBench: Benchmarking the Knowledge of LLMs in Intellectual Property (arXiv 2504.15524 v2, 29 Sep 2025)
frontier_evidence.models_tested: 17 LLMs including GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen2.5-72B, Llama3.1-70B, QwQ-32B; zero-shot, few-shot and CoT
frontier_evidence.finding: Table 4, CPC exact / CPC subclass: DeepSeek-V3 9.5 / 65.2; DeepSeek-R1 8.5 / 63.2; GPT-4o 3.3 / 62.0; GPT-4o-mini 0.5 / 52.7. IPC exact DeepSeek-R1 10.8. These are not HUPD results.

frontier_evidence.source: Large Language Models, Encoder Architectures and Hybrid Approaches for Patent Classification (arXiv 2601.23200)
frontier_evidence.models_tested: BERT-for-Patents and other encoders; open LLMs including a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B (LoRA details not stated on the page)
frontier_evidence.finding: Abstract says the best encoder outperforms the best LLM and that encoders use one to two orders of magnitude less energy at inference. No accuracy or macro-F1 numbers were in the page read. Search snippet says encoders win on frequent CPC subclasses and LLMs on rare ones.

counterevidence.note: A fine-tuned 9B LLM is beaten by a fine-tuned encoder on aggregate CPC results. The tuned-LLM route is weaker here, which lowers the case for an SLM over a classical classifier. Numbers unread.
At subclass level GPT-4o reaches 62.0%, so frontier models are far better at the broad level than at exact codes. Exact-match is where a tuned model has room to help.

small_model_evidence.finding: Encoder models beat the best LLM on aggregate CPC subclass results. The small encoder route is supported, but the numbers were not read.

candidates.why_ft_beats_rag: CPC subclass assignment is a learned mapping from patent language to a fixed taxonomy; retrieval over patent text finds similar patents, but the label convention is what the model must learn. Evidence here is weak: the one 2026 paper favours encoders, so a decoder SLM may not be the right tool.
candidates.example_input: Title: 'Wireless sensor node with adaptive duty cycling'. Abstract: '...'. Claim 1: 'A sensor node comprising a radio transceiver and a controller configured to...'.
candidates.example_output: {"cpc_subclass": "<4-character code from the HUPD cpc_labels field>"} (illustrative; take real labels from HUPD rows)
candidates.behavior_spec: For each held-out application, the model returns a CPC subclass that exactly matches the record's main_cpc_label subclass; pass means exact subclass match. Target: beat IPBench's zero-shot frontier CPC subclass figure (65.2% for DeepSeek-V3) on HUPD held-out data, with the same prompt family.
candidates.agentic_demo: 1) Read title, abstract and claims from a filing packet. 2) SLM proposes the CPC subclass and two alternates with a confidence. 3) Tool call to a CPC scheme lookup (official CPC scheme service, not read) to confirm the code exists and to fetch the group title. 4) Route to an examiner-style review queue with the evidence sentence. 5) Store the decision with the source application number.
candidates.eval: Exact subclass match and top-3 match on held-out HUPD applications with the main_cpc_label as ground truth, plus per-class macro-F1 to show the rare-class behaviour the 2026 paper highlights. Compare base, tuned and frontier models on identical prompts.
candidates.risks: HUPD licence is in conflict (CC BY-SA 4.0 in the YAML, NonCommercial in the card body), which matters if the output is commercial. Labels are the filed CPC of 2004–2018 applications, which drift from current CPC. The best evidence favours encoders, not the decoder SLM this brief asks for.
candidates.qlora_feasibility: Data is huge (125 GB) so a subset is needed; fits a 4-day timebox only with a sampled slice. The strongest published result is for encoders, so an SLM choice needs a justification against that evidence. Frontier numbers in IPBench use a different dataset.
